analysis.one_liner: Makes companies that move jobs to low-wage countries pay severance, benefits, and lose federal contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced, referred to the Senate Labor Committee, and got one hearing in April 1992, but never received a committee vote or floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted companies that close a US plant or lay off workers and move the same work to a country where average wages are less than half the US level. It would have forced those employers to give workers 120 days' notice, a week of severance pay per year of service, a year of continued health coverage, and up to $10,000 for retraining or relocation. It would also have fined employers up to $10,000 per day for skipping notice, put violators on a public Labor Department list for five years, and made listed employers lose priority for federal contracts and eligibility for federal grants and loan guarantees. Workers and the Labor Secretary could sue to enforce it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at plants closed or laid off in connection with a move of that work overseas would get four months' notice, severance of one week's pay per year worked, a year of continued health coverage, and up to $10,000 for retraining or relocation. Communities and other workers would gain from the required advance notice, and honest employers would gain federal contracting preference over companies on the relocation list.

how_it_helps.text: Covered employers must give affected workers and the Labor Secretary a 120-day relocation notice before a closing or mass layoff, with a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per day for violating it.
Dislocated workers must receive severance equal to one week of average pay per year of employment, 12 months of continued health coverage, and retraining or relocation reimbursement of up to $10,000.

Federal agencies must give contract preference to employers not on the relocation list, and listed employers become ineligible for federal grants and guaranteed loans, with narrow waivers for national security, jobs, or environmental reasons.

Employers who fail to provide notice or benefits are liable to workers for lost pay and benefits, interest, equal liquidated damages, and attorney's fees, and any worker or the Labor Secretary can sue.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that close US plants or conduct mass layoffs while moving that work to countries with average wages below half the US level. They would bear notice costs, severance and health coverage obligations, retraining reimbursements, potential fines of up to $10,000 per day, litigation exposure, and reduced access to federal contracts, grants, and guaranteed loans for five years.

drawbacks.text: The mandates raise the cost of relocating production abroad, which critics say can push companies toward automation or foreign competitors instead of saving jobs, and the costs can ultimately affect the remaining business and its prices.

The bill only covers moves to countries whose average wage is below half the US average, so offshoring to higher-wage countries such as Canada, Japan, or much of Western Europe would fall outside it entirely.

Private lawsuits with double damages and fee-shifting, plus daily fines, create significant litigation risk for employers even over good-faith disputes about whether a layoff was related to an overseas move.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers facing a plant closing tied to offshoring, the benefits are concrete and substantial: months of notice, a year of health coverage, and real money for retraining. The cost falls narrowly on companies that move jobs to very low-wage countries, though the bill might not save those jobs — it mostly makes companies pay for eliminating them. The threshold design (only countries under half US wages, employers of 25 or more) leaves many offshoring moves and small-plant closings uncovered, so it is a targeted remedy rather than a broad one.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee: referred in March 1992, got one subcommittee hearing in April, and was never voted on before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the Save American Jobs Act on March 4, 1992, joined by Senators Wofford and Riegle.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
The Labor Subcommittee held a hearing on April 7, 1992 (printed as S.Hrg. 102-550), but the committee never marked up the bill and the full Senate never voted on it.
The bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that move US production to low-wage countries are better off, since they never faced the notice, severance, and benefits obligations or the five-year blacklist from federal contracts and loans. Workers whose jobs were offshored in the interim received only whatever the existing WARN Act required — no extended health coverage, severance mandate, or retraining reimbursement from the relocating employer.

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Save American Jobs Act on March 4, 1992.

for.name: Senate Subcommittee on Labor
for.role: Subcommittee of the Labor and Human Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Held the bill's only hearing on April 7, 1992.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; after one subcommittee hearing, no markup or committee vote was ever scheduled, and the Senate never voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor signed on; the record contains no votes, so no partisan split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and other employers offshoring production to low-wage countries
industries.note: These employers would have faced 120-day notice duties, severance and health coverage mandates, daily fines for violations, and a five-year loss of federal contract preference and grant or loan eligibility when they moved work to countries paying less than half US wages. Their cost of eliminating US jobs would have risen sharply.

industries.industry: Federal contractors and grant or guaranteed-loan recipients
industries.note: Firms that did not relocate would gain a preference in federal contracting over blacklisted relocators; firms that did relocate would lose access to federal grants and guaranteed loans for five years, subject to narrow waivers.

The Secretary would have gained new duties: compiling and publishing the relocation list, investigating complaints, and suing violators, funded through new administrative and enforcement responsibilities.
